title: Anthropic Files for IPO, Setting Stage for a Trillion-Dollar AI Debut
summary: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence powerhouse behind the Claude chatbot, took a major step toward becoming a publicly traded company on Monday, filing confidentially for an initial public offering in the United States. The move sets up a high-stakes test of whether investor enthusiasm for AI can match the sector's sky-high valuations. The company did not reveal how many shares it plans to sell or at what price. Such confidential filings allow firms to prepare for an IPO while shielding sensitive financial details. Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in a late-May funding round, surpassing rival OpenAI. It reported annualized revenue of $47 billion, yet like many AI pioneers, it continues to lose money—fueling concerns of an AI bubble. Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has become a symbol of the AI boom that is reshaping industries. Its rapid ascent earlier this year rattled markets, triggering sell-offs in software stocks as investors feared its increasingly autonomous tools could disrupt traditional business models. Now, Anthropic is in a race with OpenAI and Elon Musk's SpaceX to tap public markets. 'OpenAI and Anthropic are in a race to go public before capital runs out,' said Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson. He added that going first would let Anthropic 'set the agenda for how a frontier model reports financials.' The combined demand for capital from these three giants could strain markets, Luria noted, giving an early mover a crucial advantage. At nearly $1 trillion, Anthropic's listing would vault it into the top tier of the S&P 500, alongside elite companies that dominate global equity markets. For investors, the IPO represents a chance to buy into the AI revolution—but also a gamble on whether these companies can eventually turn their massive revenues into profits.
why_it_matters: Anthropic's IPO could reshape how quickly advanced AI is funded and deployed across industries, affecting everything from how students learn to what jobs exist in the future. If the market bets correctly, AI might accelerate problem-solving in medicine and climate; if it is a bubble, a crash could freeze AI development and affect the broader economy.

background_read: Anthropic is an artificial intelligence company founded in 2021 by former executives of OpenAI (the creator of ChatGPT). It is best known for its chatbot Claude, a direct competitor to ChatGPT.

Initial public offerings (IPOs) allow companies to sell shares to the public for the first time. Tech IPOs can be huge events; for example, Facebook raised $16 billion in 2012, and Alibaba raised $25 billion in 2014. A nearly $1 trillion valuation would make Anthropic one of the most valuable companies ever to go public.

Analyst Gil Luria works for DA Davidson, a financial services firm that provides research on technology companies. The S&P 500 is a stock market index that tracks 500 large publicly traded U.S. companies; entering it instantly makes a stock a core holding for many investment funds.

The AI industry has seen a massive influx of investor money, but most AI firms are unprofitable, spending billions to develop models. This has drawn comparisons to the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when many internet companies with little to no profit went public at bonkers valuations and later crashed.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is separately planning its own IPO, although it is a space exploration and satellite company rather than a pure AI firm. Together, Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX could absorb a huge amount of available investment capital in a short time.

perspectives.description: Going public could give Anthropic a massive cash injection to research safer, more capable AI. For ordinary investors, it means a chance to own a piece of one of the most important technology companies of this decade. Successful AI firms could boost economic growth and create new industries.

A company valued at nearly $1 trillion while losing money echoes past speculative frenzies. If the AI bubble bursts, it could wipe out retirement savings and damage trust in tech innovation. Critics also worry that an IPO pushes short-term profits over long-term AI safety research.

The rush of AI companies to IPO mirrors historical patterns in silicon valley: when capital costs rise, firms seek public markets. The size of these offerings might strain overall market liquidity, potentially making it harder for other companies to raise money. The real test is whether AI can transition from costly research to mainstream moneymaker, similar to how the internet moved from dial-up to indispensable utility.

A public Anthropic would face more scrutiny from regulators, possibly accelerating calls for AI safety laws. It might also set standardized financial reporting for AI firms, making it easier to compare the true costs of building frontier models. In the coming years, the IPO’s success or failure will likely influence how much society trusts big tech and how quickly governments act to oversee AI.
